title: Cleansing, False Prophets, and a Struck Shepherd
overview: Zechariah pictures a coming day when God washes his people clean, ends idol worship and lying prophecy, and brings them through a painful testing that leaves them truly his.

parts.label: A fountain for cleansing (v. 1)
parts.note: After the people's mourning at the end of chapter 12, God promises a flowing spring that washes away both wrongdoing and the uncleanness that, under Israel's worship rules, kept people from coming near God. Christians have often read this fountain in light of Jesus' death, as forgiveness opened to everyone.

parts.label: Idols and false prophets removed (vv. 2-3)
parts.note: Even the names of idols will be forgotten, and anyone still claiming to speak for God will be treated as a liar. The picture of parents killing their own child draws on a law in Deuteronomy against anyone leading people away from God; it stresses that loyalty to God outranks family, but it is a violent image and the text does not soften it.

parts.label: Prophets ashamed to be prophets (vv. 4-6)
parts.note: A rough hair cloak was a prophet's traditional look, like Elijah's, so here pretend prophets drop the costume and insist they are just farmers. The wounds may be cuts some prophets made on themselves in frenzied rituals, which the man explains away as injuries from friends, though scholars are not sure what is meant.

parts.label: The shepherd struck (v. 7)
parts.note: God calls a sword against his own shepherd, a leader close to him, and the flock scatters, echoing the shepherd scenes in chapter 11. Jesus quotes this line the night of his arrest about his followers scattering, and Christians read it as pointing to his death, while who the shepherd was in Zechariah's own time is debated.

parts.label: A third refined by fire (vv. 8-9)
parts.note: The text plainly says two thirds of the land's people will die and one third will survive, to be tested the way metal is heated to burn off what is impure. Whether this describes a past disaster or one still to come is uncertain, but the stated goal is a restored bond in which God claims the survivors as his people and they claim the LORD as their God.

disagreement: Christians differ over whether the struck shepherd of verse 7 was mainly a direct prediction of Jesus' death or first described a leader in Zechariah's own setting that Jesus later applied to himself.
think: Can going through hardship actually make a person or a community better, or does that idea sometimes excuse suffering that should never have happened?
